unit_description: This unit teaches students to compare fractions that have the same denominator. Students use visual models, number lines, comparison symbols, and justify answers.
unit_goals: Compare fractions with the same denominator using visual models.
Compare fractions with the same denominator on number lines.
Solve comparison problems and justify answers.
Understand that with like denominators, the larger numerator names the larger fraction.

weeks.weekly_focus: Students compare fractions with the same denominator using models, number lines, and symbols.

lessons.fact_drill: Warm up by shading fraction models and comparing the shaded amounts.
lessons.concept: When fractions have the same denominator, the parts are the same size. Compare the number of shaded parts. The fraction with more shaded parts is larger.
lessons.practice: Compare fractions with like denominators using area models.
lessons.objective: Compare fractions with the same denominator using visual models.

questions.hint: Compare the shaded parts; same denominator.

learn.title: Compare Fractions Using Visual Models
teaching_points: Same denominator means same size parts.
Compare the number of shaded parts.
More shaded parts means a larger fraction.

try_it.title: Try one together
try_it.hint: 3 shaded parts is less than 5 shaded parts.

practice_block.title: Practice Time
practice_block.instructions: Use visual models to compare each pair of fractions.

flashcards.title: Like Denominators Models
flashcards.instructions: Review comparing fractions with like denominators using models.

bigIdea.title: Compare Fractions Using Visual Models
bigIdea.subtitle: More parts means bigger
bigIdea.intro: When two fractions have the same denominator, the pieces are the same size. The fraction with more pieces shaded is the larger fraction.
bigIdea.bigQuestion: Why can you compare numerators when denominators are the same?

ruleCards.description: Same denominator means each part is the same size.
More shaded parts means the fraction is larger.

lessons.fact_drill: Warm up by locating and comparing two fractions on a number line with the same denominator.
lessons.concept: On a number line, a fraction farther to the right is larger. With the same denominator, the fraction with the greater numerator is farther right.
lessons.practice: Compare fractions with like denominators on number lines.
lessons.objective: Compare fractions with the same denominator on number lines.

questions.prompt: Which is farther right on a number line: 2/7 or 5/7?
On a number line, is 4/6 to the right of 2/6?

learn.title: Compare Fractions Using Number Lines
teaching_points: Locate both fractions on the same number line.
The fraction farther right is larger.
With the same denominator, compare numerators.

example.prompt: Compare 2/5 and 4/5 on a number line.

try_it.title: Try one together
try_it.prompt: Compare 3/8 and 7/8 on a number line.

practice_block.title: Practice Time
practice_block.instructions: Use number lines to compare each pair of fractions.

flashcards.title: Like Denominators Number Lines
flashcards.instructions: Review comparing fractions on number lines.

bigIdea.title: Compare Fractions Using Number Lines
bigIdea.subtitle: Farther right means larger
bigIdea.intro: A number line shows which fraction is larger by its position. The fraction farther to the right is larger. With like denominators, this is the one with the larger numerator.
bigIdea.bigQuestion: How does a number line show which fraction is greater?

starTip.title: Right is more
lines: The one on the right is larger

ruleCards.description: Both fractions use a number line with the same denominator.
The point farther right is the greater fraction.

lessons.fact_drill: Warm up by reviewing <, >, and = symbols.
lessons.concept: The symbol < means less than, > means greater than, and = means equal to. Compare the numerators of fractions with the same denominator and choose the correct symbol.
lessons.practice: Write <, >, or = to compare fractions with like denominators.
lessons.objective: Use <, >, and = to compare fractions with like denominators.

learn.title: Use <, >, and =
teaching_points: Point the symbol toward the smaller number.
Open side points to the larger number.
Use = when the fractions are the same.

practice_block.title: Practice Time
practice_block.instructions: Write the correct symbol for each pair of fractions.

bigIdea.title: Use <, >, and =
bigIdea.subtitle: Point the symbol to the smaller number
bigIdea.intro: Comparison symbols show which fraction is larger or smaller. The open side of the symbol always points to the greater number.
bigIdea.bigQuestion: Which way does the < symbol point?

ruleCards.description: The symbol points to the smaller number.
The open side faces the larger number.

lessons.lesson_title: Solve Comparison Problems and Justify Answers
lessons.fact_drill: Warm up by comparing fractions in word problem contexts.
lessons.concept: Comparison problems ask which amount is larger or smaller. Use the same-denominator rule: compare numerators. Then justify the answer by explaining that the parts are the same size, so more parts means more.
lessons.practice: Solve word problems comparing fractions and justify answers.
lessons.objective: Solve comparison problems and justify answers.

warmup.title: Luma Charge
warmup.instructions: Warm up with fraction comparison word problems.

questions.prompt: Sam ate 3/8 of a pizza. Mia ate 5/8. Who ate more?
A rope is 2/6 blue and 4/6 green. Which color is more?
Tara ran 7/10 of a mile. Ben ran 4/10. Who ran less?

learn.title: Solve Comparison Problems and Justify Answers
teaching_points: Find the fractions in the problem.
Compare numerators because denominators are the same.
Explain why the larger numerator means more.

example.prompt: Lily colored 3/8 of a page and Alex colored 5/8. Who colored more?

try_it.title: Try one together
try_it.prompt: A jar is 4/7 full of red marbles and 3/7 full of blue marbles. Which color has more?

practice_block.title: Practice Time
practice_block.instructions: Solve each comparison problem and explain your answer.

bigIdea.title: Solve Comparison Problems and Justify Answers
bigIdea.subtitle: Explain why the larger numerator wins
bigIdea.intro: To justify a comparison, explain that the denominators are the same, so the pieces are the same size. The fraction with more pieces is larger.
bigIdea.bigQuestion: How do you justify that 5/8 is greater than 3/8?

ruleCards.description: The pieces are the same size.

lessons.fact_drill: Rapid review of comparing with models, number lines, symbols, and word problems.
lessons.concept: Review the four big ideas from this unit: comparing fractions using visual models, comparing on number lines, using comparison symbols, and solving comparison problems with justification.
lessons.practice: Complete a balanced evaluation covering the skills from this unit.
lessons.objective: Show what you know about comparing fractions with like denominators.

warmup.title: Luma Charge
warmup.instructions: Get ready to show what you know.

questions.prompt: A pie is cut into 6 slices. Ana ate 2/6 and Ben ate 4/6. Who ate more?

learn.title: Ready to Show What You Know
teaching_points: Use any strategy that helps you.

example.prompt: You have learned four big ideas this unit.
example.equation: models + number lines + symbols + word problems = like denominators

try_it.title: Try one together
try_it.prompt: Compare 5/9 and 2/9 using a number line.

practice_block.title: Unit Evaluation
practice_block.instructions: Answer all questions carefully to show your understanding.

flashcards.title: Unit 31 Review
flashcards.instructions: Review key terms from Unit 31 before the evaluation.

bigIdea.title: Unit Evaluation: Like Denominators
bigIdea.subtitle: Show what you know
bigIdea.intro: This evaluation checks your understanding of the four big ideas from this unit: comparing fractions using visual models, comparing on number lines, using < > and =, and solving comparison word problems.
bigIdea.bigQuestion: What do you know about comparing fractions with like denominators?

ruleCards.description: The fraction with more parts is larger.
Use symbols to record the comparison.
